nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FORECASTING ALGORITHMS — CASES 0, 1, 2}}

Predict $y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t}$ — often the ultimate goal. At time $t$ define the \textbf{forecast function}\[ f_t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad f_t(h) = \hat y_{t+h\mid t}, \]i.e.\ $f_t(h)$ is the $h$-step-ahead forecast made using information up to $t$.


The formulas belwo actually derive from SSM ! 

\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
 & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 0 (SES)}} \textit{(no trend, no seasonality)} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 1 — Holt}} \textit{(add trend)} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 2 — Holt-Winters}} \textit{(add seasonality)} \\
\textbf{Forecast} $\hat y_{t+h\mid t}$ & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t$ \;\textit{(flat)} & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t + h\, B_t$ \;\textit{(level + slope $\times h$)} & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t + h\, B_t + S_{t+h-m}$ \;\textit{(level + slope + seasonal at matching period)} \\
\textbf{State} $L_t$ \textit{(level)} & $L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, L_{t-1}$ & $L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})$ — \textit{use best yesterday prediction} & $L_t = \alpha\,(y_t - S_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})$ — \textit{avoid double counting} \\
\textbf{State} $B_t$ \textit{(slope)} & — & $B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1}$ — \textit{B is the average change in the last day and in the past} & $B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1}$ \\
\textbf{State} $S_t$ \textit{(seasonal)} & — & — & $S_t = \gamma\,(y_t - L_{t-1} - B_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma)\, S_{t-m}$ --- \textit{S is the average of this period's seasonal deviation (today's observation minus the predicted non-seasonal part $L_{t-1} + B_{t-1}$) and the seasonal factor one full cycle ago $S_{t-m}$} \\
\textbf{Recursive form of} $\hat y$ & substitute $\hat y_{t\mid t-1} = L_{t-1}$ into the state update: $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1}$ & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = L_t + B_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + B_t$ & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = L_t + B_t + S_{t+1-m} = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + B_t + (S_{t+1-m} - S_{t-m})$ \\
\textbf{Forecast-error correction} & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + \alpha\,(y_t - \hat y_{t\mid t-1})$ & — & — \\
\hline
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$L_t$ and exponential smoothing.}} The simplest forecast is just a \emph{weighted average of past observations with geometrically decreasing weights} (not a regression --- the weight parameter $\alpha$ is fixed, not estimated): \[ \underbrace{\hat y_{t+1\mid t}}_{L_t} \;=\; \alpha\, y_t \;+\; \underbrace{\alpha(1-\alpha)\, y_{t-1} \;+\; \alpha(1-\alpha)^2\, y_{t-2} \;+\; \dots \;+\; \alpha(1-\alpha)^{t-1}\, y_1}_{(1 - a) \hat y_{t-1\mid t-2 = L_{t-1} } } , \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1, \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \alpha\,  (1-\alpha)^k \underbrace{=}_{t \to \infty}\; 1.\]

You can always apply this to compute Lt, but it will be correct only in he Case 0

nodes.content:
In SES: 
$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 1$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx y_t$ (follows the data)

$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 0$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx$ constant

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Choosing $\alpha$ — grid search.}} Try a grid $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.99\}$. For each $\alpha$, compute the one-step-ahead forecasts on held-out data and evaluate one of:

\textbf{MAE} (Mean Absolute Error):\[ \mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| y_t - \hat{y}_t \right| \]

\textbf{MSE} (Mean Squared Error):\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left( y_t - \hat{y}_t \right)^2 \]

\textbf{MAPE} (Mean Absolute Percentage Error):\[ \mathrm{MAPE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_t - \hat{y}_t}{y_t} \right| * 100\% \]

Pick $\hat\alpha = \arg\min_\alpha \mathrm{(MAE\, /\, MSE\, /\, MAPE)}$. MAE is robust to outliers, MSE penalises large errors more heavily, MAPE is scale-free but blows up when $y_t \approx 0$.

nodes.title: Time series as stochastic processes
Markov Property
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MARKOV PROPERTY}}

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{9a.} A discrete-time stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$ with $Y_t \in \mathcal{Y}$ is \textbf{Markov} if

$\bullet$ $Y_0 \sim p_0(\cdot)$ \;(initial distribution), and

$\bullet$ for every $t \ge 1$, $Y_t\;\big|\; Y_{t-1},  \;\perp\!\!\!\perp\; (Y_0, Y_1, \dots, Y_{t-2}) $, that is $p(y_t \mid y_{0:t-1}) = \underbrace{p(y_t \mid y_{t-1})}_{\text{Transition Probability}}.$

\end{keydef}

Note how this is always big Y.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DAG view.}} A Markov chain is naturally drawn as a directed acyclic graph (DAG):\[ Y_0 \to Y_1 \to Y_2 \to \dots \to Y_{t-1} \to Y_t \to \dots \]\emph{Reading the DAG:} if you remove the node $Y_{t-1}$, the node $Y_t$ becomes disconnected from $(Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-2})$. Graphically, $Y_{t-1}$ d-separates $Y_t$ from its earlier ancestors — exactly the conditional-independence statement above.

**\textbf{9b.} Plugging the Markov property into the privous chain:** 

$\bullet$ \emph{Non-homogeneous case} (transition kernel varies with $t$):
\[ p_n(y_0, \dots, y_n) = p_0(y_0) \prod_{t=1}^{n} p_t(y_{0:t-1}) \; \underbrace{=}_{\text{Markov}}\; p_0(y_0) \prod_{t=1}^{n} p_t(y_t \mid y_{t-1}). \]


**\textbf{9c.}Specifying the Probability law of a markov process**

So the law of the process is fully specified by

$\bullet$ the \textbf{initial distribution} $p_0(\cdot)$ of $Y_0$;

$\bullet$ the family of \textbf{one-step transition proabilities} $\{p_t(y_t \mid y_{t-1}) : t \ge 1\}$.




**\textbf{9d.} The transition matrix in the finite state space**
Finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. The transition probabilities at time $t$ are\[ p^{(t)}_{i,j} = P(Y_t = j \mid Y_{t-1} = i), \qquad i, j \in \mathcal{Y}. \]Arrange them in a matrix $\mathbf{P}^{(t)}$ 

Drop t everywhere if homogeneous.

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t - 1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ & $2$ & $\cdots$ & $N$ \\
\hline
$1$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,N}$ \\
$2$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,N}$ \\
$\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\ddots$ & $\vdots$ \\
$N$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,N}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\textbf{Row-stochastic:} each row sums to 1, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} p^{(t)}_{i,j} = 1$ for every $i$ and every $t$ — given that you are in state $i$ at $t-1$, you must end up \emph{somewhere} at time $t$.

2. Recall \[ (n_{i,1}, \dots, n_{i,M}) \;\sim\; \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_{i,+};\ p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}). \]Note: $n_{i,+}$ is itself random, since it depends on how often the panel visits state $i$.


3. Define:
\[ \underbrace{ \varphi_i}_{\text{average number of times an individual will visit i in the full T span}} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{M} \eta_h \sum_{t=1}^{T} p^{(t-1)}_{h,\, i}}_{\text{imagine the transition matrix at each t}} \]
Note each state is i, the transitions are instead i to j .
$$\frac{n_{i,+}}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \varphi_i \quad$$
\[ \text{so } n_{i,+} \approx \underbrace{n\, \varphi_i}_{\text{$n_{i,+}$ = total visits to state $i$ (across all $n$ individuals, at times $0$ to $T-1$)}} \]

4. Conditional on $n_{i,+}$ known,we have an asymptotical multivariate gaussian for $j, h = 1, \dots, M$, $j \neq h$,\[ \mathbb{E}(\hat p_{i,j}) = p_{i,j}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\ \hat p_{i,h}) = -\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}}, \] 
\textit{Asymptotic confidence intervals.} A level-$(1-\alpha)$ CI for $p_{i,j}$ is\[ \boxed{\;\hat p_{i,j} \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}}\;} \]

nodes.title: Estimation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. ESTIMATION OF THE UNKNOWN PARAMETERS}}

We estimate the unknown parameters $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$ of an HMM by \emph{maximum likelihood}. Focus on the \emph{discrete non-parametric case}: $Y_t \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, latent states $S_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Write the likelihood}} 
\[ L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \]
\emph{A direct evaluation of such joint probability may be involved, because the temporal dependence of the process $(Y_t)$ may be complex. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2.Marginalize it}} 
\[ P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{a sum over all possible paths}}\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T},\, S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Bayes}}\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid S_{0:T} = s_{0:T},\, \phi)}_{(\mathrm{A})\,\text{ obs.\ given path}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{P(S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi)}_{(\mathrm{B})\,\text{ path probability}}. \]

Explaining notation: The sum is over all $K^{T+1}$ possible state paths $(s_0, s_1, \dots, s_T)$. So we have T+1 terms, each can take K values. 
Fortunately, after extracting latents, we can exploit the conditional independence structure of the HMM.} We derive it step by step.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Compute $(\mathrm{A})$ via conditional independence of observations.}} The slice notation is shorthand for the joint event, then apply chain rule, then HMM emission assumption (each $Y_t$ depends only on its own $S_t$ given the path):
\[ (\mathrm{A}) \;=\; P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid S_{0:T} = s_{0:T},\, \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{unpack slice}}\; P(Y_1 = y_1,\, Y_2 = y_2,\, \dots,\, Y_T = y_T \mid S_{0:T} = s_{0:T},\, \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}}\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(Y_t = y_t \mid Y_{1:t-1} = y_{1:t-1},\, S_{0:T} = s_{0:T},\, \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{emission CI}}\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(Y_t = y_t \mid S_t = s_t,\, \phi) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Compute $(\mathrm{B})$ via Markov property of the chain.}} The slice notation is shorthand for the joint event, then apply chain rule, then HMM Markov assumption (each $S_t$ depends only on $S_{t-1}$):
\[ (\mathrm{B}) \;=\; P(S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{unpack slice}}\; P(S_0 = s_0,\, S_1 = s_1,\, \dots,\, S_T = s_T \mid \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}}\; P(S_0 = s_0 \mid \phi) \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(S_t = s_t \mid S_{0:t-1} = s_{0:t-1},\, \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Markov}}\; P(S_0 = s_0 \mid \phi) \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(S_t = s_t \mid S_{t-1} = s_{t-1},\, \phi) \;=\; \pi_{s_0} \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 5 --- Combine.}} Multiply $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{B})$ inside the sum:
\[ \boxed{\; L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{\pi_{s_0}}_{\text{initial}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}}_{\text{transitions}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}}_{\text{emissions}}  \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T}} \pi_{s_0}\, p_{s_0, s_1}\, b_{s_1, y_1}\, p_{s_1, s_2}\, b_{s_2, y_2}\, \cdots\, p_{s_{T-1}, s_T}\, b_{s_T, y_T}. \qquad (2) \;} \]


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Maximisation.}} The MLE is $\hat\phi = \arg\max_{\phi} L(\phi \mid y_{1:T})$. Direct numerical maximisation is feasible but expensive; in practice, the EM algorithm (\emph{Baum-Welch} for HMMs) is the standard iterative procedure.



\emph{Exercise.} Write the expression of the likelihood in the discrete parametric case, assuming that the emission distribution is Poisson.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Solution.}} Parametric emission: replace the matrix $B$ with one rate per state, $Y_t \mid S_t = k, \phi \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_k)$, so $\phi = (\pi, A, \lambda_{1:K})$. Only the emission factor in Step 3 changes; Step 4 is unchanged. Substituting into (2):
\[ \boxed{\; L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{\pi_{s_0}}_{\text{initial}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}}_{\text{transitions}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{e^{-\lambda_{s_t}}\, \lambda_{s_t}^{y_t}}{y_t!}}_{\text{Poisson emissions}}. \;}\]

nodes.title: Decoding / filtering
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

Estimate the latent state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given observed $y_{1:T}$ (treat $s_0$ as fixed, and $\phi$ as known or replaced by its MLE).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, pick the marginally most likely state:
\[ s_t^* \;=\; \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s), \qquad \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). \]
\emph{Issue.} The resulting sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may include zero-probability transitions ($p_{i,j} = 0$), making the global path infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the path that maximises the joint conditional probability:
\[ \max_{s_{0:T}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi). \]
Given the data, and the parameters, what is the most likely hidden state? 

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
\[ \begin{aligned} & P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi)\, P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} \]
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi)$ wrt phi. Now we need to optimize the same thing by $S_{0:T}$

nodes.title: Exercise — weather/activity filtering (state is unobserved)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXERCISE --- Filtering: weather $\to$ activity}}

\textbf{Setup.} A person's daily activity depends on the weather, which is hidden. We observe only the activity.

$\bullet$ Hidden $\mathcal{S} = \{1 = \text{sunny},\, 2 = \text{rainy}\}$ ($K = 2$), observed $\mathcal{Y} = \{1 = \text{walk},\, 2 = \text{shop},\, 3 = \text{clean}\}$ ($M = 3$).

$\bullet$ Initial $\pi = (P(S_1 = \text{sunny}), P(S_1 = \text{rainy})) = (0.6,\, 0.4)$.

\textbf{Transition matrix} $A$ (rows = state at $t-1$, columns = state at $t$):
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & sunny & rainy \\ \hline sunny & $0.7$ & $0.3$ \\ rainy & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{Emission matrix} $B$ (rows = state, columns = activity):
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc} $S_t \backslash Y_t$ & walk & shop & clean \\ \hline sunny & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\ rainy & $0.1$ & $0.4$ & $0.5$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The universal recipe (forward algorithm).}} Define
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;:=\; P(S_t = j,\; y_{1:t}) \quad\text{(joint "score": data observed so far AND being in state $j$ now)}. \]
One rule for every step:
\[ \boxed{\; \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{today's evidence}} \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{yesterday's belief, pushed forward through } A}, \qquad \alpha_1(j) \;=\; \pi_j\, b_{j, y_1}. \;} \]
\emph{In words:} transition the old belief through $A$, then weight by today's emission. Past observations are never thrown away --- they live inside $\alpha_{t-1}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(a) After $y_1 = \text{walk}$.}} No transition needed yet (start of chain):
\[ \alpha_1(\text{sunny}) = \pi_{\text{sunny}}\, b_{\text{sunny, walk}} = 0.6 \cdot 0.6 = 0.36, \qquad \alpha_1(\text{rainy}) = 0.4 \cdot 0.1 = 0.04. \]
Walking is far more compatible with sunny ($0.6$ vs $0.1$) $\Rightarrow$ score ratio $9{:}1$ in favour of sunny.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(b) After $y_2 = \text{shop}$.}}

\emph{Predict $S_2$ from history:} push $\alpha_1$ through $A$:
\[ \text{pred}_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.7 + 0.04 \cdot 0.4 = 0.268, \qquad \text{pred}_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.3 + 0.04 \cdot 0.6 = 0.132. \]
\emph{Weight by today's emission:}
\[ \alpha_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.268 \cdot 0.3 = 0.0804, \qquad \alpha_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.132 \cdot 0.4 = 0.0528. \]
Shopping is mildly more compatible with rainy ($0.4$ vs $0.3$), pulling the belief from $9{:}1$ down to roughly $1.5{:}1$; sunny stays ahead because the chain is sticky ($p_{\text{sunny}, \text{sunny}} = 0.7$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ Two-step recipe at every $t$: (1) push the old belief through $A$ to get the predicted prior; (2) multiply by the emission to fold in today's evidence.

$\bullet$ $\alpha_t(j) = P(S_t = j, y_{1:t})$ is a \emph{joint}, not a posterior. Their relative magnitudes already tell you which state is more likely; summing them gives the data likelihood $P(y_{1:t}) = \sum_j \alpha_t(j)$ for free.

$\bullet$ This is exactly the \emph{forward algorithm} --- the engine inside HMM likelihood evaluation, filtering, and (with a small modification: $\max$ instead of $\sum$) Viterbi decoding.

nodes.title: State space models (SSM)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATE SPACE MODELS (SSM)}}



\begin{keydef}
**15** \textbf{State-space model (SSM).} An SSM is a dynamic system of stochastic processes \textcolor{blue}{(with a \emph{finite discrete} latent state space:)}
\[ \underbrace{(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}}_{\text{state process (incl.\ }\theta_0\text{)}}, \quad \underbrace{(Y_t)_{t \ge 1}}_{\text{observation process}} \quad \textcolor{blue}{(\text{HMM: }(S_t)_{t \ge 0}, (Y_t)_{t \ge 1})}, \]


where the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} state process $(\theta_t)$. In particular :

$\bullet$ $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$ **is a Markov process** with continuous state space $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$ \textcolor{blue}{(\emph{finite discrete} state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$)}, initial distribution $\pi$ and transition kernel $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ (\textcolor{blue}{transition \emph{matrix} $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$, $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$}).


$\bullet$ Given $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are **conditionally independent** and each $Y_t$ **depends only on** $\theta_t$:
\[ p(y_t \mid \theta_{0:t}, y_{1:t-1}) = p(y_t \mid \theta_t). \]
\textbf{Equivalently,} the law of an SSM is fully specified by:
\[ \theta_0 \;\sim\; \underbrace{\pi}_{\text{initial law}}, \qquad  \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \;\sim\; \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})}_{\text{transition kernel}}, \qquad Y_t \mid \theta_t \;\sim\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)}_{\text{emission kernel}}, \]


\textcolor{blue}{\emph{HMM version of the law:}
\[ S_0 \;\sim\; \pi, \qquad S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \mathrm{Categorical}(p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}), \qquad Y_t \mid S_t = j \;\sim\; p(y_t \mid \theta_j^*). \]}
\end{keydef}




\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Example of Parametric emission --- Poisson emissions.}} In other cases one may want a parametric emission distribution, so that $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$, $j = 1, \dots, K$. For example, for the earthquakes data (unbounded counts), one could assume
\[ Y_t \mid (S_t = j) \;\sim\; \text{Poisson}(\theta_j^*), \]
that is, at state $j$, $Y_t$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\theta_j^*$. Note how the parameter can switch across states!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this fixes the plain-Poisson defects.}} A single Poisson forces (i) mean $=$ variance, (ii) no serial dependence. Letting the rate \emph{switch} with a Markov chain breaks all three:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Different mean and variance per regime.} Within state $j$, both equal $\lambda_j^*$, but across regimes they differ --- a "quiet" state has small mean \emph{and} small variance, an "active" one has large mean \emph{and} large variance.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation.} Sticky regimes ($p_{j,j}$ near $1$) mean neighbouring $Y_t$'s likely share the same rate, so
\[ \text{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \text{Cov}(\lambda_{S_t}^*, \lambda_{S_{t+h}}^*) \;>\; 0. \]
No additive $\epsilon$ needed --- the dependence comes from persistence of the hidden chain.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN STATISTICS --- Bayes' rule, derivation and intuition}}

You forecast the next value to be A. But you want to deal with uncertainty... the soltuon is probability

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The goal.}} We want to know
\[  P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \]
i.e.\emph{"after seeing evidence $B$, how likely is hypothesis $A$?"}. 
\emph{The problem.} The joint $P(A \cap B)$ is usually hard to compute directly. Bayes' rule is the trick to express it in terms of quantities we can compute.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{From the definition of conditional probability.}} For two events $A, B$,
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B \mid A) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}. \]
merge out the intersection: 
\[ \underbrace{P(A \mid B)}_{\text{posterior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{after} seeing } B} \;=\; \frac{\overbrace{P(B \mid A)}^{\text{likelihood: how compatible } B \text{ is with } A}\, \cdot \overbrace{P(A)}^{\text{prior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{before} seeing } B}}{\underbrace{P(B)}_{\text{evidence: marginal probability of } B}}. \]

Bayes is a form of learning from experience! 


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key reformulation --- the "evidence multiplier".}} Rewrite Bayes as
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; P(A) \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{P(B \mid A)}{P(B)}}_{\text{evidence multiplier}}. \]

Clearly the denominator is a normalization. That is this event happens with 3% probablity in eenral, when A is active, 4% so this evidence is aligned with A being active. Notcie, aybe youhave prior of 90% that somebody is guilty then you get a very irrelevatn test that with 5% probability fires guilty in generla, and ot tis  guy it fired 5.1%.d oes htis mea tha tthe probabioty of him biegn guilty is now 5.1%? no! you had other proofs that had ocmposed that 90% and this extra evidence is a tiny little new proof in favour of him beign gy8itly




\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why Bayes' rule is brilliant.}} The genuine insight is the \emph{change of perspective}:
\[ \underbrace{P(A \cap B)}_{\text{hard to compute directly}} \;\;\longleftrightarrow\;\; \underbrace{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}_{\text{both easy: a model + a prior}}. \]
You see, an hard co-occurence problem has been simplified to a conditional probablity (derivable from an experiment) and a prior. 



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Concrete example --- medical test.}}

$\bullet$ Disease prevalence: $P(D) = 0.01$.

$\bullet$ True positive rate: $P(+ \mid D) = 0.99$.

$\bullet$ False positive rate: $P(+ \mid \neg D) = 0.05$.

\emph{Question:} A patient tests positive. What is $P(D \mid +)$?

Bayes:
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{P(+ \mid D)\, P(D)}{P(+)}. \]
Denominator (law of total probability):
\[ P(+) \;=\; P(+ \mid D)\, P(D) + P(+ \mid \neg D)\, P(\neg D) \;=\; 0.99 \cdot 0.01 + 0.05 \cdot 0.99 \;=\; 0.0594. \]
So
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{0.99 \cdot 0.01}{0.0594} \;\approx\; 0.167. \]

\emph{Reading.} Even with a "99\% accurate" test, a positive result means only $\approx 17\%$ chance of having the disease --- because the disease is rare to start with. The prior $P(D) = 0.01$ is so small that the evidence multiplier $P(+ \mid D)/P(+) = 0.99 / 0.0594 \approx 16.7$ only pushes the posterior to $0.01 \times 16.7 \approx 0.17$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Core Bayesian idea.}} Evidence must be interpreted \emph{relative to the baseline frequency}. Rare priors require strong evidence to overturn.

nodes.title: Bayesian vs frequentist inference
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN vs FREQUENTIST INFERENCE}}

After deriving Bayes' rule and seeing the prior get \emph{updated} by evidence into a posterior, a natural question arises: \emph{does the prior shift mean there is no true $\theta$?} The answer is no --- but to see why, we need to compare the two frameworks side by side.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The status of $\theta$.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist.} $\theta$ is a \textbf{fixed unknown constant} of nature. It does not have a probability distribution. Probability is reserved for the data. Not a random variable. Ucertainty is driven by the samplig procedure (we see a different estimate just because the sample is not fully representative of the population)"$P(\hat\theta \in [a, b]) = 0.95$" means: if we repeated the sampling many times, 95\% of the resulting intervals $[\hat a_n, \hat b_n]$ would contain the true $\theta$. Estimator: MLE. 


$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian.} $\theta$ may also be a fixed unknown constant in nature --- but since we don't \emph{know} it, we represent our \textbf{state of belief} about $\theta$ as a probability distribution: $\pi(\theta)$ before data, $p(\theta \mid y)$ after. The randomness lives in our \emph{knowledge} (is epistemic), not in $\theta$ itself. $\theta$ is a **random variable.**  Estimator: Posterior. 

So the prior shifting does \emph{not} mean $\theta$ moves. It means our \emph{uncertainty about $\theta$} sharpens around the values most compatible with the data. The true $\theta$ (if you believe in one) is a fixed point in parameter space; the probability mass representing our knowledge is what slides around it.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Confidence intervals (frequentist) vs Credible intervals (Bayesian).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Frequentist confidence interval --- exact formula.}} Given an estimator $\hat\theta_n$ with (asymptotic) standard error $\text{SE}(\hat\theta_n)$ (how the estimator estimates would vary across replicaitons of the experiment, derived analytically from the model), the $1 - \alpha$ Wald confidence interval is
\[ \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \bigl[\, \hat\theta_n - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat\theta_n),\;\; \hat\theta_n + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat\theta_n) \,\bigr], \]
where $\text{SE}(\hat\theta_n) = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$., and $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard Normal (e.g.\ $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ for 95\%).





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayesian credible interval --- exact formula.}} A $1 - \alpha$ credible interval is any interval $[a, b]$ such that the posterior probability
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WORKED EXAMPLE --- RW + noise with fixed hidden state}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}} The local-level state-space model with state-noise variance fixed to $W = 0$ (so $w_t = 0$ a.s.\ and the state is constant: $\theta_t = \theta_0 \equiv \theta$ for all $t$):

$\bullet$ \emph{State equation (degenerate random walk):} $\theta_t \;=\; \theta_{t-1},\qquad \theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0).$

$\bullet$ \emph{Observation equation:} $Y_t \;=\; \theta + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \theta.$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Goal.}} Compute the posterior $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n})$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reminder --- Gaussian density (kernel form).}} A $\mathcal{N}(m,\, C)$ density evaluated at $x$ (mean $m$, variance $C$) is
\[ \mathcal{N}(x;\, m,\, C) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi C}} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{(x - m)^2}{2 C}\Bigr). \]
For matching coefficients, we will repeatedly use the kernel-in-$\theta$ form (everything not involving $\theta$ goes into the normalising constant):
\[ \mathcal{N}(\theta;\, m,\, C) \;\stackrel{\theta}{\propto}\; \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\theta^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{C} \;-\; 2\theta \cdot \tfrac{m}{C}\bigr]\Bigr). \]

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l}
Step & Non-recursive (batch) & Recursive (one-step-at-a-time) \\
\hline
\emph{Bayes setup} & iid factorises the likelihood: \;$f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \prod_{t=1}^{n} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta).$ &\;$f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto f(y_n \mid \theta_n) \cdot f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1}) $ with $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1}) = \mathcal{N}(m_{n-1}, C_{n-1})$:  \\
\hline
\emph{Step 1 - plug in Gaussians} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_t - \theta)^2\bigr) \cdot \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta - m_0)^2}{2 C_0}\bigr).$ & $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(y_n - \theta_n)^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigr) \cdot \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta_n - m_{n-1})^2}{2 C_{n-1}}\bigr).$ \\
\hline
\emph{Step 2 - collect $\theta^2,\, \theta$ terms} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \stackrel{\theta}{\propto} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\theta^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta\bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr).$ & $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \stackrel{\theta_n}{\propto} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\theta_n^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr).$ \\
\hline
\emph{Step 3 - match the kernel} $(m, C)$ & $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}; \quad m_n = C_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\bigr).$ \;Equivalently: \;$C_n = \tfrac{C_0\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}, \quad m_n = \tfrac{\sigma^2\, m_0 + n\, C_0\, \bar y}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}.$ & $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}; \quad m_n = C_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr).$ \;Equivalently: \;$C_n = \tfrac{C_{n-1}\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + C_{n-1}},\quad m_n = \tfrac{\sigma^2\, m_{n-1} + C_{n-1}\, y_n}{\sigma^2 + C_{n-1}}.$ \\
\hline
\emph{Result} & $\boxed{\; \theta \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n) \;}$ with the closed-form $(m_n, C_n)$ above. & $\boxed{\; \theta_n \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n) \;}$ obtained by iterating the recursion $n$ times from $(m_0, C_0)$. \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TABLE 5 --- Composite models (built by stacking simpler DLMs).}}

\emph{Adjust preamble accordingly.}  &  $\bullet$ $\theta$: 3D, $(T_t, C_t, C_{t-1})$, aux det., $p = 3$.

nodes.title: SSM flexibility — no stationarity required
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SSM FLEXIBILITY --- why no stationarity requirement}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why ARMA cannot fit a non-stationary series.}} ARMA models a process with \emph{constant} parameters $(\phi_i, \theta_j, \sigma^2)$. A model with constant parameters can only describe data whose statistical properties are themselves constant in time: constant mean, constant variance, autocovariance depending only on the lag. That is exactly the definition of weak stationarity.

If the data is non stationary: has a trend (mean drifting upward), seasonality (mean cycling), or changing volatility (variance growing), there is \emph{no choice} of constants $(\phi_i, \theta_j, \sigma^2)$ that can reproduce it --- because constants cannot represent a moving target.  



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Intuition --- model the system, not the symptoms.}} ARMA describes how $Y_t$ correlates with its own past, summarised by a few constants; that only works if those correlations don't drift. SSMs describe \emph{what is, endogenously, producing} $Y_t$ --- a latent dynamical system whose own evolution can have trend, drift, seasonal swings, regime switches.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Aside --- if you let ARMA's parameters drift, you get an SSM.}} The cleanest way to see SSM as the strict superset of ARMA is to let the ARMA coefficients become time-varyin!

nodes.title: Example 3: AR(1) (A and B)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 3 --- AR(1), continuous-state Markov (A: directly observed; B: SSM lift).}}


\textbf{7. Steps:} 
\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} Discrete-time Markov process on $\mathbb{R}$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \varphi\, Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]
Note the use of big Y as this is a structural statement. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof: $|\varphi| < 1$ $\Rightarrow$ weakly stationary.}} Unroll the recursion from $Y_0$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \varphi^t Y_0 \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, \varepsilon_{t-k}. \]
\emph{1.\ Constant mean.}
\[ E[Y_t] \;=\; \underbrace{\varphi^t\, E[Y_0]}_{\to 0 } \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, E[\varepsilon_{t-k}]  \;=\; \varphi^t\, E[Y_0] \;+\; \underbrace{0}_{E[\varepsilon]=0}\cdot\frac{1-\varphi^t}{1-\varphi} \;=\; 0 \]

\emph{2.\ Constant, finite variance.} By independence of shocks and $Y_0$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \underbrace{\varphi^{2t}\, \mathrm{Var}(Y_0)}_{\to 0 } \;+\; \sigma^2 \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^{2k} \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{1-\varphi^2} \qquad \text{for all } t. \quad \checkmark \]

Note how you could have started also from a non stationary Y0 and gained asymptotic stationarity

\emph{3.\ Autocovariance depends only on lag $h$.} For $h \ge 0$:
\[ \gamma(h) \;:=\; \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \varphi^h\, \gamma(0). \]No $t$-dependence. \quad $\checkmark$
depends only on the lag! 

\emph{Autocorrelation:} $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0) = \varphi^{h}$ 


SO: IT IS STATIONARY!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

nodes.title: Probability vs Likelihood
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Probability vs likelihood --- one formula, two readings.}}

The expression $P(B \mid A)$ is \emph{literally} the same number whether you call it a probability or a likelihood. There is no different formula and no proportionality involved:
\[ L(A; B) \;=\; P(B \mid A). \]
The only thing that changes is what you keep fixed and what you treat as the argument:

$\bullet$ \emph{Probability reading.} $A$ is fixed, $B$ varies. Evaluating $P(B \mid A)$ tells you how likely each potential outcome $B$ is, under the assumed hypothesis $A$. Used for \emph{forward prediction}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Likelihood reading.} $B$ is fixed at the data we actually observed, $A$ varies. Now $P(B \mid A)$ is read as a function of $A$ --- it scores how well each candidate hypothesis explains the observed $B$. This is the reading in the Bayes context. 

depends on what data you observe and what is unknowns! (or you have both)

nodes.title: Smoothing and decoding
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SMOOTHING (and a note on DECODING) --- DLMwR Sec.\ 2.7.4 / pp.\ 60--63.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Smoothing:} $\boxed{\,\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}),\quad t < T\,}$ --- \emph{past} state given \emph{ALL} the data, including observations after $t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Kalman smoother --- one backward pass, two possible outputs.}}

\emph{Inputs (run forward filter first and store).} Filtering moments $(m_t, C_t)$ and predicted-state moments $(a_{t+1}, R_{t+1})$ for every $t = 0, \dots, T$.


\emph{Backward pass} for $t = T-1, T-2, \dots, 0$ --- choose one of two modes:

\textbf{(A) Analytical marginals} $\theta_t \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(s_t, S_t)$ (Prop.\ 2.4, p.\ 61):
\[ s_t \;=\; m_t + J_t\, (s_{t+1} - a_{t+1}), \qquad S_t \;=\; C_t - J_t\, (R_{t+1} - S_{t+1})\, J_t^\top. \]
\emph{The smoother gain (shared by both outputs):}
\[ \boxed{\; J_t \;=\; C_t\, G_{t+1}^\top\, R_{t+1}^{-1}. \;} \]
$J_t$ is the regression coefficient of $\theta_t$ on $\theta_{t+1}$ in their joint Gaussian distribution --- the backward analog of the Kalman gain.

\emph{Reading $s_t$ component-wise.} $s_t$ is just the vector of \emph{component-wise expected values} of the state given all data:
\[ s_t \;=\; E[\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}]. \]
If, e.g., $\theta_t = (\alpha_t,\, \beta_t)^\top$ (described by the component equations $\alpha_t = \dots$, $\beta_t = \dots$), then
\[ s_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} E[\alpha_t \mid y_{1:T}] \\ E[\beta_t \mid y_{1:T}] \end{pmatrix}. \]
Each entry of $s_t$ is the posterior mean of the corresponding state component conditional on the full data record. Same for $S_t$: the $(i,i)$ entries are the marginal variances $\mathrm{Var}(\theta_{i,t} \mid y_{1:T})$, off-diagonals the covariances.

\emph{Initialise at $t = T$:} the last time-point has no future, so smoothing $=$ filtering: $s_T = m_T,\; S_T = C_T$, or sample $\theta_T \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof of the analytical-marginal formulas (RTS).}}

\emph{(i) Marginalisation + chain rule.}
\[ \pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})  \; \underbrace{=}_{\text{ Marginalisation + chain rule}}\; \int \underbrace{\pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:T})}_{\pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:t}) \text{ by (1)}} \, \pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta_{t+1} \]
(1) Given $\theta_{t+1}$, the future observations $y_{t+1:T}$ add no information about $\theta_t$


\emph{(ii) Compute the backward kernel $\pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t})$ via Bayes (likelihood $\times$ prior):} 
\[ \pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \overbrace{\pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t,\, y_{1:t})}^{\text{likelihood, simplify:} \pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)}\, \overbrace{\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})}^{\text{prior}} \]

 Both factors are Gaussian (read off the filter and the model):
- From the state equation gaussiani + $G_{t+1}\theta_t$ fixed once you now $\theta_t$. \[ \pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t) = \mathcal{N}(G_{t+1}\theta_t,\, W_{t+1})\]
- This you already know: 
\[\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) = \mathcal{N}(m_t, C_t). \]
Note how you would have an expected value as mean instead. 

(iii) By Gaussian conditionting, with $J_t = C_t\, G_{t+1}^\top\, R_{t+1}^{-1}$:
\[ \theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:t} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\, m_t + J_t(\theta_{t+1} - a_{t+1}),\;\; C_t - J_t\, G_{t+1}\, C_t \,\bigr). \]

\emph{(iv) Take expectation and variance of the integral (tower rules).}

\emph{Mean.} $\;s_t = E[\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}] = E\bigl[E[\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t}] \mid y_{1:T}\bigr] = E\bigl[m_t + J_t(\theta_{t+1} - a_{t+1}) \mid y_{1:T}\bigr]$
\[ \;=\; m_t + J_t\, (s_{t+1} - a_{t+1}), \]
using $E[\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:T}] = s_{t+1}$. \quad $\checkmark$

\emph{Variance.} Law of total variance:
\[ S_t \;=\; E\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t}) \mid y_{1:T}\bigr] + \mathrm{Var}\bigl(E[\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t}] \mid y_{1:T}\bigr). \]
The first term is constant (the conditional variance doesn't depend on $\theta_{t+1}$): $C_t - J_t G_{t+1} C_t$. The second is $\mathrm{Var}(J_t \theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:T}) = J_t S_{t+1} J_t^\top$. So
\[ S_t \;=\; C_t - J_t\, G_{t+1}\, C_t + J_t\, S_{t+1}\, J_t^\top. \]
Use $J_t G_{t+1} C_t = J_t R_{t+1} J_t^\top$ (since $J_t = C_t G_{t+1}^\top R_{t+1}^{-1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $J_t R_{t+1} = C_t G_{t+1}^\top$ $\Rightarrow$ $J_t R_{t+1} J_t^\top = C_t G_{t+1}^\top J_t^\top = J_t G_{t+1} C_t$) to rewrite:
\[ S_t \;=\; C_t - J_t\, (R_{t+1} - S_{t+1})\, J_t^\top. \quad \checkmark \]

nodes.title: Posterior mean and precision
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior precision $1/C_n$.}} The precision \emph{adds}:
\[ \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_n}}_{\text{posterior precision}} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_0}}_{\text{prior precision}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n}{\sigma^2}}_{\text{data precision}}. \]
The lower the variance of Cn th ebetter! Because both terms are non-negative, $1/C_n \ge 1/C_0$ always --- the posterior is \emph{always} at least as precise as the prior. Even poor-quality data (large $\sigma^2$) adds some information, just less of it. Sharper data ($\sigma^2$ small) or more data ($n$ large) makes the posterior sharper.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior mean $m_n$ as a weighted average.}} Rewrite $m_n$:
\[ m_n \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1/C_0}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{prior weight}} \cdot m_0 \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{data weight}} \cdot \bar y. \]
$m_n$ is a convex combination of the \emph{prior mean} $m_0 = E[\theta]$ and the \emph{sample mean} $\bar y$, with weights proportional to the respective precisions (frequentist would just have used the sample mean).

nodes.title: SSM filtering and prediction
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CHEATSHEET --- inference formulas, side-by-side (Case A vs Case B)}}

\emph{Notation.} \textbf{Case A} = iid observations given a static $\theta$ (textbook conjugate setting; no time evolution of the parameter). \textbf{Case B} = SSM with time-varying latent state $\theta_t$ (Markov dynamics, here illustrated with the local-level / RW + noise model).

About filterign and prediction: Kalman derived it in a totally different way, it did a recursive least stare estimation (regression). Later, this derivation, that is fully bayesian came. Note how you (1) start by applyign the bayes rule and (2) we treat $\theta_t$ as random and compute its full posterior distribution $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, not just a point estimate or a sampling distribution of an estimator.



\begin{tabular}{p{2.5cm}|p{10cm}|p{7cm}}
Topic & \textbf{Case A} (iid / static $\theta$) & \textbf{Case B} (DLM / linear-Gaussian SSM) \\
\hline
\emph{1. Filtering: posterior of state given data up to now} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:T}) \;\underbrace{\propto}_{\text{Bayes}}\; f(y_{1:T} \mid \theta)\, f(\theta) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{unpack slice}}\; f(Y_1 = y_1,\, \dots,\, Y_T = y_T \mid \theta)\, f(\theta) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{chain, conditioned on }\theta}\; \Bigl[\prod_{t=1}^{T} f(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1},\, \theta)\Bigr]\, f(\theta) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{iid}\,|\,\theta\,\text{ or Markov ppt (DAG)}\,\Rightarrow\, Y_t \,\perp\, Y_{1:t-1}\,|\,\theta}\; \Bigl[\prod_{t=1}^{T} f(y_t \mid \theta)\Bigr] \cdot f(\theta)$ & Trick: $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}) = f(\theta_t \mid y_t,\, y_{1:t-1}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t,\, y_{1:t-1})}_{ f(y_t \mid \theta_t) \quad \text{single new emission}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{* \quad \text{predicted prior}}.$. You can prove the joint is normal Gaussian. \emph{Why not use the Case A procedure verbatim? **}. *$f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;\underbrace{=}_{(Marginalization)}\; \int f(\theta_t,\, \theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{(Chain)}\; \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1},\, y_{1:t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{(Markov)}\; \int \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})}_{\text{transition}}\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{\text{yesterday's posterior}}\, d\theta_{t-1}$.
\emph{Interpretation.} Today's predicted state distribution $=$ average (integral) of the transition probabilities from yesterday to today, weighted by yesterday's posterior --- "where you were yesterday."
 \\

\\
\hline
\emph{2. One-step state prediction} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})$ unchanged (static state) & $f(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}) = \int f(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)\, \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\,}_{\text{filter}} d\theta_t$ \; \\
\hline
\emph{3. $h$-step state prediction} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})$ unchanged. Static state $\Rightarrow$ $\theta_{T+h} \equiv \theta$ at every horizon $h$. & ${\; f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Marginalization}}\; \int f(\theta_{t+h},\, \theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Chain}}\; \int f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1},\, y_{1:t})\, f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Markov}}\; \int \underbrace{f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1})}_{\text{transition}}\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})}_{(h{-}1)\text{-step prediction}}\, d\theta_{t+h-1}. \;}$ \\
\hline
\emph{4. $h$-step observation prediction} & $f(y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}) = \int f(y_{T+h} \mid \theta)\, f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta$ & ${\; f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Marginalization}}\; \int f(y_{t+h},\, \theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h} \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Chain}}\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t},\, \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h} \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Markov}}\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})}_{\text{filter + predict}}\, d\theta_{t+h}. \;}$
The integration variable must match what's varying in the integrand.
\emph{Reading.} \textbf{KEY:} For each candidate value of the contemporaneous state $\theta_{t+h}$, the emission gives a forecast $f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})$; we average these forecasts, weighted by how plausible each $\theta_{t+h}$ is given the data we have already seen ($f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$). \\
\hline
\emph{5a. Gaussian posterior / state forecast $\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}$} & $\theta \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T,\, C_T)$ with $C_T = \tfrac{C_0\, V}{V + T\, C_0}$, \;$m_T = \tfrac{V\, m_0 + T\, C_0\, \bar y}{V + T\, C_0}$. \;$\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} = \theta \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$ \emph{(state is constant, all horizons identical)}. & \emph{Posterior:} $\theta_T \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$. \;\emph{$h$-step forecast:} $\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(a_{T+h}, R_{T+h})$ with $a_{T+h} = G^h\, m_T$ and $R_{T+h} = G^h\, C_T\, (G^h)^\top + \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} G^j\, W\, (G^j)^\top$ \;(equivalently the recursion $a_{T+h} = G\, a_{T+h-1}$, $R_{T+h} = G\, R_{T+h-1}\, G^\top + W$; $h = 1$ recovers the one-step case). \\
\hline
\emph{5b. Gaussian predictive ($h$-step, covers $h=1$) $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}$} & $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_{T+h},\, Q_{T+h})$ with $f_{T+h} = m_T$, $Q_{T+h} = C_T + V$. \;(Same as 5b for all $h$ because the state is fixed.) & $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_{T+h},\, Q_{T+h})$ with $f_{T+h} = m_T$, $Q_{T+h} = C_T + h\, W + V$. \;Forecast bands fan out linearly in $h$. \\
\hline
\emph{5c. Filter update --- prediction-error correction form} & $m_t = m_{t-1} + K_t\, e_t$, \;$C_t = (1 - K_t)\, C_{t-1}$, \;where $e_t = y_t - m_{t-1}$ (innovation), $K_t = C_{t-1} / (C_{t-1} + V)$ (Kalman gain). \;Note $a_t = m_{t-1}$, $R_t = C_{t-1}$ (no predict step since $W = 0$). & $m_t = a_t + K_t\, e_t$, \;$C_t = R_t - K_t F\, R_t = (I - K_t F)\, R_t$, \;where $a_t = G\, m_{t-1}$, $R_t = G\, C_{t-1}\, G^\top + W$ (predict), \;$f_t = F\, a_t$, $Q_t = F\, R_t\, F^\top + V$, \;$e_t = y_t - f_t$ (innovation), \;$K_t = R_t\, F^\top\, Q_t^{-1}$ (Kalman gain). \\
\end{tabular}

\emph{Footnote on what these symbols mean.} Every $m_t, C_t, a_{t+1}, R_{t+1}, f_{t+1}, Q_{t+1}$ in the table is just a (conditional) expectation or variance:
\[ m_t = E[\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}], \;\; C_t = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}); \quad a_{t+1} = E[\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}], \;\; R_{t+1} = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}); \quad f_{t+1} = E[Y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}], \;\; Q_{t+1} = \mathrm{Var}(Y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}). \]
The "Kalman formulas" in each row are just the application of $E$ and $\mathrm{Var}$ to the state and observation equations (using linearity and independence of the noise terms).

nodes.title: Model checking: forecast errors / innovations
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MODEL CHECKING --- forecast errors / innovations.}}

Once a DLM is fit (filter run, parameters estimated), check whether the model is adequate by inspecting the one-step-ahead \emph{forecast errors} (a.k.a.\ \emph{innovations / residuals}).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Forecast error and one-step decomposition.}}

\emph{One-step forecast (Kalman):} $f_t = \mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$.

\emph{One-step forecast variance:} $Q_t = \mathrm{Var}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$.

\emph{Forecast error / innovation / residual:}
\[ \boxed{\; e_t \;=\; y_t - f_t \;=\; y_t - \mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;} \]
So we can decompose every observation as
\[ y_t \;=\; \underbrace{f_t}_{\text{forecast (known at }t-1)} \;+\; \underbrace{e_t}_{\text{innovation: the new info at }t}. \]
$f_t$ is what the model expected before seeing $y_t$; $e_t$ is the surprise.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{What well-specified residuals should look like.}}

If the model is correct, the innovations $\{e_t\}$ are \emph{independent across time} (they extract all serial information; nothing predictable left) and Gaussian:
\[ e_t \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, Q_t) \quad\text{independently across }t. \]
\emph{Standardised innovations:}
\[ \tilde e_t \;=\; \frac{e_t}{\sqrt{Q_t}} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1) \quad\text{i.i.d.} \]
This is the object you actually plot / test. Checks:

$\bullet$ \emph{Normality:} Q--Q plot of $\{\tilde e_t\}$ against $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$; Shapiro--Wilk.

$\bullet$ \emph{No autocorrelation:} ACF/PACF of $\{\tilde e_t\}$ should look like white noise; Ljung--Box test.

$\bullet$ \emph{Variance stable:} time plot of $\tilde e_t$ --- no heteroskedasticity / outliers / change-points.

If any of these fails, the model is mis-specified (wrong $G, F, V, W$, missing component, wrong noise distribution, $\dots$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Exercise (Petris Prop.\ 2.7, p.\ 73) --- the standardised innovations are iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.}}

\emph{Claim.} Under a correctly specified DLM, the sequence $\{\tilde e_t\} = \{e_t / \sqrt{Q_t}\}$ is a Gaussian white noise: iid $\mathcal{N}(0,\, 1)$.

The proof has four pieces. The key technical tool is the \emph{Law of Iterated Expectations (LIE)}: $\mathbb{E}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(X \mid \mathcal{F})]$ for any sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}$.

\emph{(i) Zero mean: $\mathbb{E}(e_t) = 0$.}

\[ \mathbb{E}(e_t) \;=\; \mathbb{E}(Y_t - f_t) \;\overset{\text{LIE}}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\bigl(Y_t - f_t \mid y_{1:t-1}\bigr)}_{\text{condition on past}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, f_t \text{ by definition}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(f_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, f_t,\text{ see below}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\, f_t - f_t\,] \;=\; 0. \]

\emph{Why $\mathbb{E}(f_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) = f_t$?} Because $f_t = \mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ is by construction a \emph{function of} $y_{1:t-1}$ (computed by the Kalman filter from data up to $t-1$). A random variable that is already determined by the conditioning sigma-algebra equals its own conditional expectation --- conditioning on what you already know doesn't change it.

\emph{(ii) Uncorrelated across time: $\mathrm{Cov}(e_t, e_s) = 0$ for $s < t$.}

\emph{Why $e_s$ is past-measurable.} For $s < t$, $e_s = Y_s - f_s$ is a function of $Y_{1:s}$ (since $f_s$ is computed by the Kalman filter from $y_{1:s-1}$). Because $s < t$, we have $\{Y_1, \dots, Y_s\} \subseteq \{Y_1, \dots, Y_{t-1}\}$, so $e_s$ is also a function of $y_{1:t-1}$. Call it
\[ e_s \;=\; g(y_{1:t-1}) \;=:\; Z. \]
So $Z$ is past-measurable (known once you condition on $y_{1:t-1}$).

\emph{Apply LIE.}
\[ \mathrm{Cov}(e_t, e_s) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t\, Z)}_{\mathrm{Cov} \,-\, \mathbb{E}(e_t)\mathbb{E}(Z),\ \mathbb{E}(e_t) = 0 \text{ by (i)}} \;\overset{\text{LIE}}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t\, Z \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{Z \text{ pulls out, past-meas.}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, Z \cdot \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, 0 \text{ as in (i)}}\,\bigr] \;=\; 0. \]
Z can be pulled out, recall it is $y_t - f_t$, so for that conditioning it is fully detemrined

\emph{(iii) Variance --- needs the \emph{law of total variance} (LTV).} For any random variable $X$ and sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(X) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(X \mid \mathcal{F})\bigr] \;+\; \mathrm{Var}\!\bigl[\mathbb{E}(X \mid \mathcal{F})\bigr]. \]
Apply with $X = e_t$, $\mathcal{F} = y_{1:t-1}$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(e_t) \;\overset{\text{LTV}}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, Q_t,\ \text{see below}}\,\bigr] \;+\; \mathrm{Var}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, 0 \text{ as in (i)}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[Q_t] \;+\; \mathrm{Var}[0] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[Q_t]. \]

\emph{Why $\mathrm{Var}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) = Q_t$?}
\[ \mathrm{Var}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; \mathrm{Var}(Y_t - f_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;\overset{(\star)}{=}\; \mathrm{Var}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; Q_t. \]
$(\star)$: $f_t$ is a constant given that conditioning.

\emph{(iv) Put it all together --- standardise.}

\emph{Conditional law.} In a Gaussian DLM, the Kalman filter gives $Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_t,\, Q_t)$. Subtract the constant $f_t$ (past-measurable):
\[ e_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, Q_t). \]
\emph{Standardise.} $Q_t$ is past-measurable $\Rightarrow$ a constant under $\mathbb{E}(\cdot \mid y_{1:t-1})$. Divide $e_t$ by $\sqrt{Q_t}$:
\[ \tilde e_t \;=\; \frac{e_t}{\sqrt{Q_t}} \;\Bigm|\; y_{1:t-1} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1). \]
\emph{Marginalise.} This conditional law does \emph{not depend on} $y_{1:t-1}$, so the marginal is the same: $\tilde e_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. Idea: if $X \mid Y$ has the same distribution for every $Y$, then $X$ is independent of $Y$, and     marginally $X$ just has that distribution. The conditioning is doing no work.

\emph{Independence.} The whole $\{e_t\}$ process is jointly Gaussian (linear combinations of jointly Gaussian $Y$'s), and by (ii) they are pairwise uncorrelated. For jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelated $\Leftrightarrow$ independent. Standardising preserves this.

\emph{Conclusion.} $\{\tilde e_t\}$ is iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. $\square$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 1 --- Simple random walk.}}

\textbf{6. Steps} 
- A player starts with capital $y_0 > 0$, **deterministic**. 
- Assume $Z_t \underbrace{\sim}_{iid} N (0, \sigma^2)$ (Gaussian RW, $Y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).$ )\[ Y_t \;=\; Y_{t-1} + Z_t \;=\; y_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{t} Z_k. \]
$Z_t$ iid and independent of past $Y$'s $\Rightarrow$ Markov|

\[ E[Y_t] \;=\; E\Bigl[\sum_{s=1}^{t} Z_s\Bigr] \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{t} E[Z_s] \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{t} 0 \;=\; 0. \]

\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\sum_{s=1}^{t} Z_s\Bigr) \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{t} \mathrm{Var}(Z_s) \;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{t} \sigma^2 \;=\; t\sigma^2. \]
\emph{Variance grows linearly in $t$} (standard deviation widens as $\sqrt{t}$),



 so the walk is \textbf{non-stationary} (note $V(Y_0) = 0$  bceause $y_0$ is fixed deterministic). The variance of the random walk explodes in time. 


\emph{Continuous-time limit} (small steps in rapid succession): \textbf{Brownian motion}. The recursion works for any iid $Z_t$, not just $\pm 1$.

nodes.title: Parameter Estimation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PARAMETER ESTIMATION}}

Estimate the \emph{fixed}, time-invariant constants $\phi$ of the model from data $y_{1:T}$. Two routes: \emph{maximum likelihood} (frequentist) or \emph{Bayesian inference}.

Two approaches
$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: maximise the likelihood over $\phi$ to get the MLE $\hat\phi$. A note on identifiability: two parameter values $\phi_1 \neq \phi_2$ may give the SAME likelihood for every possible dataset. Then the $\arg\max$ is not unique --- the model is \emph{not identifiable}. Prefer the more parsimonious model. For CI:  
\[ \sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\; I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr) \quad \rightarrow \quad \hat\theta_n \;\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}\; \mathcal{N}\!\Bigl(\theta_0,\; \tfrac{1}{n\, I_1(\theta_0)}\Bigr) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{iid}}\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\theta_0,\; I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr). \]
Hence CI:
\[ \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\theta_0) \;=\; \hat\theta_n \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{I_n(\hat\theta_n)}}  \]
For 95\%: $z_{0.975} = 1.96$. \emph{Frequentist plug-in.} Take $\hat\phi$, then compute $f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \hat\phi)$ by the rules above. \emph{Pretends $\hat\phi$ is the truth} --- forecast bands too narrow. 

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian posterior predictive.} Integrate out $\phi$:
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \phi)\, f(\phi \mid y_{1:T})\, d\phi. \]
This is just \emph{Bayes' rule applied twice}: once to get the filtered/predicted state distribution given $\phi$, then again to integrate out the parameter. Forecast bands honestly account for parameter uncertainty.

nodes.title: Examples
Bayesian point estimation: loss functions and the posterior mean
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN POINT ESTIMATION --- summary measures from a posterior via expected loss.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{When this comes up.}} \emph{Post-processing step after Bayesian inference.} You first run whatever Bayesian computation gives you a posterior --- filter for $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, Bayes' rule for $f(\theta \mid y)$, MCMC samples, etc. \emph{Then}, maybe you want to report a single number summary $\hat a$ rather than the whole distribution.
In linear-Gaussian DLMs the Kalman filter already returns this number ($m_t$) for free --- so you rarely think about the decision rule, but it is implicitly squared loss.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayes estimator (general formula).}}
L = loss fucntion
\[ \boxed{\; \hat a^* \;=\; \arg\min_{a}\, E\bigl[L(\theta, a) \mid y\bigr] \;=\; \arg\min_{a}\, \int L(\theta, a)\, f(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta. \;} \]
\emph{loss $\times$ posterior weight}, integrated over $\theta$ (we don't know $\theta$, we only have its posterior distribution).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three classic loss functions and their Bayes estimators.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Squared loss} $L(\theta, a) = (\theta - a)^2$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ $\hat a^* = E[\theta \mid y]$ (\emph{posterior mean}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Absolute loss} $L(\theta, a) = |\theta - a|$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ $\hat a^* = \mathrm{median}(\theta \mid y)$ (\emph{posterior median}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{0--1 loss} $L(\theta, a) = \mathbf{1}\{\theta \neq a\}$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ $\hat a^* = \arg\max_\theta f(\theta \mid y)$ (\emph{posterior mode = MAP}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Asymmetric loss} (e.g.\ $\alpha (\theta - a)_+ + \beta (a - \theta)_+$) $\;\Rightarrow\;$ a \emph{posterior quantile}. Common in finance / inventory / energy where over- vs.\ under-prediction cost differently.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why squared loss gives the posterior mean (1-line proof).}}
\[ E[(\theta - a)^2 \mid y] \;=\; E[\theta^2 \mid y] - 2 a\, E[\theta \mid y] + a^2. \]
Differentiate with respect to $a$ and set to zero: $-2 E[\theta \mid y] + 2 a = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat a^* = E[\theta \mid y]$. (Second derivative $= 2 > 0$: it is a minimum.)

trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TIME-SERIES INFERENCE --- PRINT-READY DOSSIER}}

\emph{Self-contained merge of nine snippets covering the SSM inference toolkit, ordered from the basic Bayesian recursion (filtering) through observation prediction, smoothing and decoding, the Gaussian closed form, and two end-to-end worked examples. Page references in the worked examples are to Petris--Petrone--Campagnoli (DLMwR).}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Table of contents.}}
$\bullet$ 1. Filtering
$\bullet$ 2. State Prediction
$\bullet$ 3. Observation Prediction
$\bullet$ 4. Smoothing and Decoding
$\bullet$ 5. Decoding --- Viterbi detail
$\bullet$ 6. Gaussian Simplification (closed-form predictive)
$\bullet$ 7. Posterior Mean and Precision (algebraic form)
$\bullet$ 8. Worked Example 1 --- RW + noise, fixed state
$\bullet$ 9. Worked Example 2 --- RW + noise, dynamic state ($W > 0$)

================================================================================

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Filtering}}


NOW WE USE BAYES RULE: 


Recall: $y_{1:T}$ is it like $P(y_1, y_2, ... y_T)$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Filtering (state estimation)} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What is the state today, given everything observed up to today?}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Generic Bayes with background --- the only formula we use.}}
\[ \boxed{\; f(A \mid B,\, C) \;\propto\; f(B \mid A,\, C)\, \cdot\, f(A \mid C). \;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First instinct: treat $y_{1:t}$ as a single blob $B$.}} Naive vanilla Bayes ($C = \emptyset$, $B = y_{1:t}$):
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_{1:t} \mid \theta_t)}_{(\star)}\, \cdot\, f(\theta_t). \]
The factor $(\star) = f(y_{1:t} \mid \theta_t)$ does not simplify, is not Markov! 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The fix: split the conditioner into background $+$ new datum.}} Don't lump $y_{1:t}$ as one blob; split it:
\[ y_{1:t} \;=\; \underbrace{y_{1:t-1}}_{\text{background } C \text{ (already conditioned on yesterday)}} \;\cup\; \underbrace{y_t}_{\text{new datum } B}. \]
Now apply the boxed conditional Bayes with $A = \theta_t$, $B = y_t$, $C = y_{1:t-1}$:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_t,\, y_{1:t-1}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t,\, y_{1:t-1})\,}_{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)} \cdot\, f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \]

 $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ is your belief about $\theta_t$ \emph{before seeing $y_t$, after having processed $y_{1:t-1}$}. 



Recalling that a bayesian forecat is: 
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} f(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $f(\theta \mid y)$.

By Markov:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1}, \]
"Today's predicted state distribution = average (intergal) of the transition probabilities form yesterday to today * yesterday's posterior (second term, where you were yesterday)

\emph{Equivalent batch form (textbook / iid case).} When $\theta$ is a \textbf{static} parameter and observations are conditionally iid given $\theta$, you can write the posterior in one shot using all data and the original prior:
\[ f(\theta \mid y_{1:T}) \;\propto\; f(y_{1:T} \mid \theta) \cdot f(\theta) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{iid}}\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot f(\theta). \]
Note: there is no iid with a time-varying $\theta_t$, and there is no identical distribution either (each $y_t$ has its own $\theta_t$).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. State Prediction}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. State prediction} $\;\;f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{Where will the hidden state be $h$ steps from now?} Just keep applying the transition kernel, no new evidence:
\[ f(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)\, \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\,}_{\text{obtained by filtering}} d\theta_t \]
and recursively
\[ f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1})\, f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1}. \]
i obtain this one step per time, so first i predict h+1 then h+2 etc. State h means h iterations. 


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. Observation Prediction}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PREDICTION --- how Bayesian concepts give us all the formulas}}

**Intro**
\emph{Where does the predictive density come from?} By the definition of a conditional density (chain rule applied to the joint of $T+1$ observations):
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \frac{f(y_{1:T+1})}{f(y_{1:T})}. \]
This is the natural starting point, BUT SAME AS BEFORE:  \emph{both} densities on the right are usually intractable directly --- each requires integrating the full joint over all latent quantities. The trick is to introduce $\theta$ (parameter or state) into the picture and marginalise it out instead, which gives the closed posterior-predictive form below. 

**General version (textbook posterior predictive)**
 For observed data $y_{1:T}$, future observation $y_{T+1}$, and latent quantity $\theta$ (parameter or state):
\[ \boxed{\; f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1},\, \theta \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{*}}\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \theta)\, f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta. \; = \; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid \theta_{T+1})\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})}_{\text{need to retrive this with filtering and}} d\theta_{T+1}. \;} \]
*you can always ask to yourself, when y takes this value, what value x takes?

Note the integration variabel must watch what's varying in the integrand. 

\emph{Reading.} **KEY**:  For each candidate value of the contemporaneous state $\theta_{T+1}$, the emission gives a forecast $f(y_{T+1} \mid \theta_{T+1})$; we average these forecasts, weighted by how plausible each $\theta_{T+1}$ is given the data we have already seen ($f(\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})$, the predicted-state distribution).



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Multi-step ahead Observation prediction} $\;\;f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What value will we observe $h$ steps from now?} Marginalise the future state out of the joint $(y_{t+h}, \theta_{t+h})$:
\[ f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h}. \]
\emph{Reading.} Plug each candidate state $\theta_{t+h}$ into the emission to get a forecast distribution conditional on that state; weight by how likely that state is given the data so far; integrate. This is the \textbf{posterior predictive} from the Bayesian-statistics snippet, applied to the SSM.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. Smoothing and Decoding}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. Smoothing} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$.} \emph{Looking back, what was the state at time $t$ given all data including the future?} Bayes again, this time using future data to refine our belief about $\theta_t$:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\cdot\; \frac{f(y_{t+1:T} \mid \theta_t)}{f(y_{t+1:T} \mid y_{1:t})}, \]
i.e.\ multiply the filtered posterior by the likelihood of the future (given $\theta_t$), then renormalise. The forward--backward algorithm computes this efficiently by running a forward filter then a backward pass.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Decoding (HMM only)} $\;\;\arg\max_{s_{0:T}} f(s_{0:T} \mid y_{1:T})$.} \emph{Most likely path of hidden states.} By Bayes, $f(s_{0:T} \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid s_{0:T})\, f(s_{0:T})$, and we already computed both factors when deriving the likelihood (equation $(2)$ in the Estimation snippet). Maximisation over $s_{0:T}$ is done by dynamic programming (Viterbi). For DLMs the joint is Gaussian and the joint mode equals the vector of marginal means --- so smoothing already gives the decoded path.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6. Likelihood (for parameter estimation)} $\;\;f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)$.} \emph{If the model has unknown parameters $\phi$.} Marginalise out the hidden path:
\[ f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;=\; \int f(y_{1:T},\, \theta_{0:T} \mid \phi)\, d\theta_{0:T}. \]
This is the building block for both:

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: maximise over $\phi$ to get the MLE $\hat\phi$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: combine with a prior $\pi(\phi)$ via Bayes' rule, $f(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)\, \pi(\phi)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Putting parameter uncertainty into prediction.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist plug-in.} Take $\hat\phi$, then compute $f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \hat\phi)$ by the rules above. \emph{Pretends $\hat\phi$ is the truth} --- forecast bands too narrow.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian posterior predictive.} Integrate out $\phi$:
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \phi)\, f(\phi \mid y_{1:T})\, d\phi. \]
This is just \emph{Bayes' rule applied twice}: once to get the filtered/predicted state distribution given $\phi$, then again to integrate out the parameter. Forecast bands honestly account for parameter uncertainty.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example (HMM weather/activity).}} The recursion we used in the filtering exercise,
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{likelihood of new obs}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{prior carried forward}}, \]
is exactly the SSM filtering formula above, with discrete states. The \emph{predict} half (the sum) propagates yesterday's belief through $\mathbf{P}$; the \emph{update} half (the multiplication by $b_{j, y_t}$) is Bayes applied to today's observation.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bottom line.}} There is only one engine: \emph{posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\cdot$ prior}, with marginalisation to remove unwanted variables. Filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding, MLE, posterior predictive --- each is just that engine pointed at a different conditional or marginal of the SSM joint.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Decoding --- Viterbi detail}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

Estimate the latent state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given observed $y_{1:T}$ (treat $s_0$ as fixed, and $\phi$ as known or replaced by its MLE).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, pick the marginally most likely state:
\[ s_t^* \;=\; \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s), \qquad \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). \]
\emph{Issue.} The resulting sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may include zero-probability transitions ($p_{i,j} = 0$), making the global path infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the path that maximises the joint conditional probability:
\[ \max_{s_{0:T}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi). \]
Given the data, and the parameters, what is the most likely hidden state? 

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
\[ \begin{aligned} & P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi)\, P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} \]
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi)$ wrt phi. Now we need to optimize the same thing by $S_{0:T}$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6. Gaussian Simplification (closed-form predictive)}}


**Closed form in the Gaussian case** 
Recall $Y_{T+1} = \theta + \varepsilon_{T+1}$
**If** the posterior of the latent is Gaussian
\[ \theta \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_T,\, C_T), \qquad  C_T \;=\; \frac{C_0\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + T\, C_0}, \qquad m_T \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2\, m_0 \;+\; T\, C_0\, \bar y}{\sigma^2 + T\, C_0}. \]
The emission is Gaussian with observation noise $\varepsilon_{T+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ ($Y_{T+1} = \theta + \varepsilon_{T+1}$ given $\theta$); the predictive distribution evaluates in closed form to
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\bigl(m_T,\; C_T + \sigma^2\bigr). \;} \]

\emph{Variance has two terms, with meanings.}

$\bullet$ $C_T$ --- \emph{parameter / state uncertainty}: we don't know $\theta$ exactly, only the posterior $\mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$.

$\bullet$ $\sigma^2$ --- \emph{future observation noise}: even if we knew $\theta$ exactly, $Y_{T+1}$ would still have noise.

Adding them is the Bayesian honesty about uncertainty: forecast bands include both. The frequentist plug-in $Y_{T+1} \mid \hat\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta, \sigma^2)$ keeps only the $\sigma^2$ term and produces bands that are too narrow. IT IS SO OBVIOUS THE FREQUENTIST IS WRONG, JUT BECAUSE BEING $\hat \theta$ ESTIMATED it cannot be used as a fixed point. Note frequentists fixed this by a correction for estiamtion uncertainty.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Beyond fixed state --- general DLM closed form.}}

The simple $\mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T + \sigma^2)$ is the \emph{fixed-state} special case. For a general DLM
\[ \theta_t = G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\; w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W), \qquad Y_t = F\, \theta_t + v_t,\; v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V), \]
the predictive is still closed-form, but with more terms.

\emph{Step 1 --- predict the state.} Push the filtered posterior through the transition:
\[ \theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(a_{T+1},\, R_{T+1}), \qquad a_{T+1} = G\, m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} = G\, C_T\, G^\top + W. \]
\emph{Scalar / local-level case} ($G = 1$): $\;a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad R_{T+1} = C_T + W.$

\emph{Simplest non-trivial $G$ ($G = 2$, scalar state doubles each step):} $\theta_t = 2\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t$. Then $a_{T+1} = 2\, m_T$ (mean doubles) and $R_{T+1} = 4\, C_T + W$ (variance scales by $G^2 = 4$, plus the new innovation $W$). \textbf{Key asymmetry:} $G$ acts \emph{linearly} on the mean but \emph{quadratically} on the variance --- because $\mathrm{Var}(c X) = c^2 \mathrm{Var}(X)$. \emph{Tiny numerical check.} If $m_T = 5,\, C_T = 1,\, W = 3$: $a_{T+1} = 10,\, R_{T+1} = 4 \cdot 1 + 3 = 7$. (An explosive model in practice, but pedagogically clean.)

\emph{2-dimensional $G$ ($G$ a $2 \times 2$ matrix --- local linear trend).} State $\theta_t = (\mu_t,\, \beta_t)^\top$: level $\mu$ and slope $\beta$. Let $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ --- the slope $\beta$ is added into the level $\mu$ each step (linear extrapolation), while the slope itself is unchanged. Suppose the filter gives $m_T = (m_\mu,\, m_\beta)^\top$ and $C_T = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} C_{\mu\mu} & C_{\mu\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} & C_{\beta\beta} \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

\emph{Predicted mean.} Multiply $G$ into $m_T$:
\[ a_{T+1} \;=\; G\, m_T \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} m_\mu \\ m_\beta \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} m_\mu + m_\beta \\ m_\beta \end{pmatrix}. \]
Reading: predicted level $=$ current level $+$ current slope (one-step linear extrapolation); predicted slope $=$ slope (unchanged).

\emph{Predicted variance.} Multiply $G$ on both sides of $C_T$:
\[ R_{T+1} \;=\; G\, C_T\, G^\top + W \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} C_{\mu\mu} + 2\, C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} & \;C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} & C_{\beta\beta} \end{pmatrix} + W. \]

\emph{Step 2 --- predict the observation.} Push the predicted state through the emission:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1}), \quad f_{T+1} = F\, a_{T+1}, \quad Q_{T+1} = F\, R_{T+1}\, F^\top + V. \;} \]
\emph{Scalar / local-level case} ($F = 1$, $V = \sigma^2$): $\;f_{T+1} = a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad Q_{T+1} = R_{T+1} + \sigma^2 = C_T + W + \sigma^2.$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{7. Posterior Mean and Precision (algebraic form)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior precision $1/C_n$.}} The precision \emph{adds}:
\[ \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_n}}_{\text{posterior precision}} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_0}}_{\text{prior precision}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n}{\sigma^2}}_{\text{data precision}}. \]
The lower the variance of Cn th ebetter! Because both terms are non-negative, $1/C_n \ge 1/C_0$ always --- the posterior is \emph{always} at least as precise as the prior. Even poor-quality data (large $\sigma^2$) adds some information, just less of it. Sharper data ($\sigma^2$ small) or more data ($n$ large) makes the posterior sharper.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior mean $m_n$ as a weighted average.}} Rewrite $m_n$:
\[ m_n \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1/C_0}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{prior weight}} \cdot m_0 \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{data weight}} \cdot \bar y. \]
$m_n$ is a convex combination of the \emph{prior mean} $m_0 = E[\theta]$ and the \emph{sample mean} $\bar y$, with weights proportional to the respective precisions (frequentist would just have used the sample mean).
